question: You downloaded a PDF lecture note from an online link, but you notice the file name ends with '.pdf.exe'. What should you do?
option_1: Open it quickly to check if the notes are inside.
option_2: Delete it immediately without opening it.
option_3: Rename it to just '.pdf' so it opens as a document.
option_4: Forward it to a friend to test if it opens on their phone.
explanation: Files ending in '.exe' are program files that can run harmful code on your computer. Hackers often add '.pdf' in front of '.exe' to trick you into opening a virus.
bonus_challenge: Do you know how to turn on 'File Name Extensions' on your computer so hidden extensions like .exe always show up?

question: You suddenly receive a text message with a login security code for your email account, but you didn't try to log in. What should you do right away?
option_1: Ignore it, because the hacker didn't get the code.
option_4: Forward the message to your friend to ask if it is real.
explanation: If you get a login code without asking for it, someone already knows your password and is trying to sign in. Changing your password immediately keeps your account safe!
bonus_challenge: Check if your email provider lets you log out of all active devices with one click!

question: You are building a simple shopping app. A user adds three items costing $10 each, but the total displays as $101010 instead of $30! What is most likely causing this bug?
option_1: The store database is temporarily offline.
option_2: The app is treating the prices as text instead of numbers.
option_3: The phone's internet connection was interrupted.
option_4: The user's phone screen resolution is too low.
explanation: When a computer program treats numbers as text (strings), using the plus sign glues the words together ('10' + '10' + '10' = '101010') instead of adding them mathematically!
bonus_challenge: What function or tool in programming would you use to convert text numbers into real integers?

question: You connect your laptop to your home Wi-Fi and see full signal bars, but no websites will load. What is most likely the issue?
option_1: The router is sending a local Wi-Fi signal, but lost its connection to the Internet provider.
option_2: Your laptop's Wi-Fi receiver is completely broken.
option_3: You entered the wrong Wi-Fi password when connecting.
option_4: Your laptop needs a network cable plugged in to browse the web.
explanation: Full Wi-Fi bars mean your laptop is successfully talking to your router locally, but the router itself isn't getting Internet service from your provider.
bonus_challenge: What quick physical test or check would you do on the router to see if the Internet cable/line is connected properly?

question: You set up a smart system to automatically water your garden every morning. However, it keeps watering even right after a heavy rainstorm! What sensor should you add so it only waters when needed?
explanation: A soil moisture sensor checks how wet or dry the dirt actually is, so the controller knows to skip watering when the soil is already wet from rain!
bonus_challenge: What threshold setting would you send to your controller to prevent the pump from turning on when it rains?

question: You turn on a heavy electric iron while running on your home solar system, and the inverter suddenly starts beeping loudly and shuts off the power. What is most likely happening?
option_1: The solar panels ran out of sunlight.
option_2: The total power drawn exceeded the inverter's limit.
option_3: The charge controller turned off the sun's energy.
option_4: The battery completely drained in one second.
explanation: Inverters have built-in overload protection. When you plug in high-wattage appliances that exceed what the inverter can safely deliver, it shuts down automatically to prevent damage.
bonus_challenge: Can you name two other everyday home appliances that draw high wattage and could trigger an inverter overload?

question: You download a free simple Flashlight app on your phone. As soon as you open it, the app asks for permission to access your contacts and phone call history. What is the safest thing to do?
option_1: Allow permissions so the app can function properly
option_2: Deny the permissions and uninstall the app immediately
option_3: Turn off your mobile data before granting permissions
option_4: Restart your phone to skip the permission pop-up
explanation: A simple flashlight app only needs control of your camera's LED light. Requesting your personal contacts and phone logs is a big red flag that the app is harvesting your private data.
bonus_challenge: Check your phone settings right now! Name one app you found that has permission to access your Location or Microphone even though it doesn't really need it.
